name: Foods Chemistry
tagline: Food composition, additives, flavor chemistry, and nutritional analysis.
seo_title: Foods Chemistry — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Foods Chemistry on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in food composition, flavour, preservation, nutrition and food safety.

definition.lead: Food chemistry studies what food is made of and the chemical changes it goes through during cooking, processing and storage.
definition.body: Why bread crust browns, why cut apples turn brown, how mayonnaise stays together and how preservatives keep food safe: it all comes down to chemistry. The field also measures nutrients, contaminants and allergens.

timeline.title: Canning
timeline.text: Nicolas Appert publishes his method for preserving food in sealed, heated containers.
timeline.why: Food could be stored for months.

timeline.title: Food adulteration exposed
timeline.text: Frederick Accum publishes a treatise on food adulteration.

timeline.title: Pasteurization
timeline.text: Louis Pasteur shows that gentle heating prevents spoilage.

timeline.title: Margarine
timeline.why: An early processed food designed by a chemist.

timeline.title: Hydrogenated fats
timeline.text: Wilhelm Normann patents the hydrogenation of liquid oils.
timeline.why: Solid fats from oils, but later concerns about trans fats.

timeline.title: Umami
timeline.text: Kikunae Ikeda identifies glutamate as the taste of kombu broth.

timeline.title: The Maillard reaction
timeline.text: Louis-Camille Maillard describes the reaction between amino acids and sugars.
timeline.why: The chemistry of browning and roasted flavour.

timeline.title: Mapping browning
timeline.text: John Hodge publishes a scheme for the Maillard reaction pathways.
timeline.why: Still the reference map for food browning.

timeline.title: Trans fat labelling
timeline.text: The United States requires trans fat content on nutrition labels.
timeline.why: Led manufacturers to reformulate many foods.

quiz.explain: It produces the brown colours and roasted flavours of cooked food.
No amino acids are needed, unlike the Maillard reaction.

quiz.q: Why do cut apples turn brown?
quiz.explain: Polyphenol oxidases react with oxygen once cells are broken.

quiz.q: Why does lemon juice slow apple browning?
options: Its acid slows the enzymes, and its vitamin C is an antioxidant
It adds a colour that hides the browning
It adds sugar that coats the surface
It heats the apple and kills the cells
quiz.explain: Lower pH and an antioxidant both help.

options: Lecithin from egg yolk acts as an emulsifier
quiz.explain: Emulsifiers sit between oil droplets and water.

quiz.q: The umami taste comes mainly from…
quiz.explain: Found in tomatoes, parmesan, soy sauce and kombu.

quiz.q: Rancidity of fats is mainly caused by…
quiz.explain: Antioxidants and cool, dark storage slow it down.

options: Heats food to kill pathogens while preserving most of its quality
Freezes food to stop bacteria growing
Adds salt to draw water out of microbes
quiz.explain: Milk is commonly heated to 72 °C for 15 seconds.

options: Starch granules absorb water and swell on heating
Starch freezes and forms ice crystals
Starch dries out and becomes brittle
quiz.explain: This is why rice and sauces thicken when cooked.

quiz.q: Partial hydrogenation of oils can create…
quiz.explain: Many countries now restrict artificial trans fats.

options: The water available to microbes and reactions
The total amount of water in a food
The pH of the water in a food
The hardness of the water used in cooking
quiz.explain: Honey contains water but has low water activity, so it resists spoilage.

quiz.q: Vanillin is the main flavour compound of…
quiz.explain: Most vanillin used today is made synthetically.
